why_this_block_exists: $format is documentation for workflow authors. The loader carries it through as JSON
but the runner does not execute it. Keep operational behavior in the real workflow
fields below; keep explanations here so the JSON stays editable without external docs.
prompt_authoring: Prompts may be a string, an array of strings, or `prompt_file`.
This file intentionally uses arrays so long prompts are readable in the workflow JSON.
The loader joins prompt arrays with newline characters. Use an empty string for a blank line.
`prompt_file` is available for operator workflows; relative paths resolve against this JSON file.
Do not convert the shipped workflows to prompt_file unless the prompt is meant to live outside
globals: `globals` holds reusable prompt fragments or include descriptors.
Steps opt in with `include`: `{{globals.name}}` is interpolated before the agent call.
An object like `{include, header}` means: load that file into the prompt context and label it
with the optional header. A string global is inlined as literal text.
Use globals for cross-step invariants that must stay consistent, such as commit message style
and the rule that deterministic workflow steps own git/make/publish.
defaults: `defaults` supplies step fields when a step omits them.
Here the default agent is slow, the default mode is coding, each eval gets three attempts,
and exhausting those attempts fails the workflow.
`eval.on_fail.on_exhausted` override the defaults for that step only.
ordering_and_parallelism: The runner dispatches a step only after every id in `depends_on` has completed.
`run_if` and `skip_if` are evaluated after dependencies complete; skipped steps do not run.
Normal fix steps are sequential because each step depends on a concrete prior artifact.
Parallelism is represented by `lenses`: one step prompt runs once per lens concurrently,
then the lens outputs are merged according to `aggregate`. The fix review step uses
parallel lenses so each reviewer gets an independent context window.
Do not add prompt-level reviewer checklists or alternate review steps to fix.json.
The only supported fix-review shape is this JSON `review` step with `lenses`,
failure_and_retries: A step with `eval` first produces outputs, then the eval decides whether those outputs are
acceptable. Passing eval records the accepted effect before deterministic reaper steps run.
Failing eval follows `eval.on_fail.action`: `repeat` reruns the same step, `branch_to` moves
control back to another step and invalidates dependent work, `continue` keeps going, and
`max_attempts` limits eval failures for that step. When it is exhausted, `on_exhausted`
chooses the final control action, otherwise the workflow default applies.
Driver errors before usable outputs are produced use the step eval retry budget when an
eval block is configured; otherwise they fail immediately unless the driver owns a retry path.
eval_control_flow: Evals are the bridge between JSON outputs and workflow control flow.
`field_check` evaluates an expression over workflow outputs, for example
`builtin` runs a named Rust validator for reusable workflow safety contracts.
`judge_llm` sends the step outputs plus `judge_prompt` to an agent and expects
Branching evals are how compile/review failures send the workflow back to `write-patch`
without letting the model mutate git directly.
fix_shape: Research decides whether the bug is real. Invalid finding_dir inputs terminally update
the finding metadata via a reaper step.
When valid, write-patch changes files, fixes-tag-search proves provenance,
write-commit-message writes .kres-commit-msg.tmp, commit creates/amends the git commit,
build compiles the target, triage decides whether compile failures are patch errors,
review proves the patch and commit message claims, and publish exports the final diff.

title: Fix a kernel bug
description: Research the bug, write a patch, commit it, build it, review it, and publish it. Deterministic reaper steps handle status edits, git, make, and patch export.

globals.output_rules: Never paste a unified diff or .patch as code_output content. Edits go through code_edits (or code_output rewriting the same file). Diffs are produced by `git diff HEAD~1` after the commit lands. Deterministic workflow steps own git add, git commit, git commit --amend, workspace build, and publish; do not emit mutating git/build/publish followups from LLM steps. Keep analysis tight; the artifacts are the diff and the commit message.
globals.self_fix_trap: Once code_edits or a git commit have landed, the files on disk contain YOUR work. Reading them back and seeing the fix in place is not evidence of upstream prior art. [INVALID] requires a file:line or commit ref that existed BEFORE this run started.

steps.title: Research the bug
prompt: You are running the kres FIX flow, step 1: RESEARCH.
BUG INPUT: {{workflow.target}}
KIND: {{workflow.target_kind}}
FIX RUN MODE: {{workflow.fix_run_mode || 'standalone'}}
BROADER FIX SERIES PLAN, IF THIS IS A PER-TODO RUN:
{{workflow.fix_series_plan || ''}}
CURRENT FIX TODO, IF THIS IS A PER-TODO RUN:
{{workflow.current_fix_todo || ''}}
CURRENT FIX PLAN REVISION: {{workflow.fix_plan_revision || '0'}}
PRIOR RESEARCH ATTEMPTS FROM THIS RUN (oldest first; empty on first attempt):
{{research.prior_attempts || ''}}
If non-empty, each entry is a previous slow-agent JSON output for this same step that
failed the eval. For ambiguous bugs with several plausible fix shapes, do not propose a
fourth different shape every retry — that is fix-shape thrashing, not progress.
Read the prior fix_plan and prior research_decision; commit to one of the proposed
shapes by gathering the specific evidence that would prove its fix_contract, OR
explicitly justify in analysis why a new shape is now correct (cite concrete source
or commit evidence that ruled the prior shape out). If a prior attempt's blocking
followups were not gathered, finish gathering them before proposing a new shape.
Research has two modes with separate authority:
- Planning mode: when CURRENT FIX TODO is empty, determine whether the input contains
one bug or multiple independently committable bugs. Create fix_plan as an ordered
array of todos, one per commit. Every todo must have id, title, scope, affected_files,
affected_symbols, fix_contract, rationale, and depends_on fields. Use one item for
a single-commit fix only when the finding has one coherent failure mode and one
coherent patch/review surface. Use multiple todos when the input describes multiple
independently triggerable failures, multiple affected sites with different fix
contracts, or changes that should be reviewed, retried, built, and published
independently. Do not collapse todos merely because each individual commit leaves
the overall finding partly unfixed; series commits may be complementary. If a later
todo depends on an earlier one to compile, be safe, or make semantic sense, encode
that ordering in depends_on instead of merging them into one todo. For invalid or
unconfirmed research, fix_plan may be omitted or empty.
Also emit bug_inventory with one stable id and description per original distinct bug.
Bug identity is independent of commit decomposition: multiple fix_plan todos may
address one bug, and one todo may contribute to multiple bugs. When metadata.bugs
exists, preserve those exact ids and descriptions in bug_inventory.
- Per-todo mode: when CURRENT FIX TODO is non-empty, verify only that todo against
workspace HEAD and return research fields scoped to that todo. Keep fix_plan equal
to the broader series plan so later steps understand the surrounding series, but do
not broaden affected_files, affected_symbols, or the fix contract beyond the current
todo.
If the bug is proven but the current todo's fix contract is wrong or incomplete,
set research_status=unconfirmed, set research_decision.bug_proven=true,
fix_contract_proven=false, invalidity_proven=false, and return fix_plan with a
revised version of the current todo using the same id. Put the corrected scope,
affected files/symbols, fix_contract, rationale, and depends_on in that typed
todo. You are not the series planner in this mode: do not add, remove, reorder,
split, or merge other todos unless the evidence requires a typed plan_update. Rust may replace the current todo and rerun it; do not rely on prose to
carry the correction.
When evidence requires changing the remaining graph, emit plan_update with
expected_revision equal to CURRENT FIX PLAN REVISION and ordered operations.
Supported operations are replace_current(todo), split_current(todos),
append_after_current(todos), revise_pending(todo), and remove_pending(id).
Completed todos are immutable. Every resulting dependency must still name an
earlier todo. Use plan_update only with research_status=unconfirmed; Rust validates
and atomically applies the complete update before rerunning from the current index.
If KIND is finding_dir, read FINDING.md, summary.md, and metadata.yaml from the target
before doing anything else. metadata.yaml.git.sha is the audit's HEAD; the workspace
HEAD may differ. If the affected symbols changed since that sha, verify the bug still
exists. If those files cannot be read, do not declare the bug invalid; request the
missing read access/context instead.
metadata.yaml status: a metadata.yaml that says `status: invalidated` (or `confirmed`,
`unconfirmed`, `confirmed_latent`, etc.) is a stale snapshot written by an earlier run.
It is informational, not authoritative. The authoritative source of truth is current
code at workspace HEAD plus reachable in-tree history. If you verify the alleged bug
is present in the source at workspace HEAD, set research_status=confirmed and proceed
with the fix even when metadata.yaml says `invalidated` — the publish step rewrites
metadata.yaml when the patch lands, so the yaml will end up reflecting the new
reality. Only set research_status=invalid when source or commit evidence (not the yaml
status field) proves the bug does not exist. Cite the specific file:line or commit SHA
in invalid_evidence. Treating the yaml status as invalidating evidence is the failure
mode where a bug really fixed by a prior run gets re-invalidated on every subsequent
audit instead of being recognised as already-fixed (which is a different invalidation
shape: cite the actual fix commit, not the yaml).
Commit SHAs found in metadata.yaml, summary.md, FINDING.md, auto-generated-fix*.diff,
or any other artifact file are hints only. They have no permanence until they are
reachable from the source workspace's Git history. A commit object existing locally,
`git show <sha>` succeeding, or an artifact patch beginning with `From <sha>` does
NOT prove the fix is in workspace HEAD; it may be an orphaned generated commit, a
commit from another clone, or a stale patch file. To decide whether a cited commit
is present in the current source tree, use this bounded recipe:
1. `git show -s --oneline <sha>` only checks that the object exists.
2. `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> HEAD` is the authoritative reachability test
for whether the commit is included in workspace HEAD (exit 0 means yes).
3. If the ancestry check fails, inspect the current source directly and treat the
SHA/patch metadata as stale unless the current code independently has the same
semantic fix.
Do not infer ancestry from an empty `git log <sha>..HEAD`; that range can also be
empty when HEAD is an ancestor of <sha>. When checking whether an existing patch
already handles the bug, require a combination of commit reachability (when a SHA
is cited), subject/message match, and semantic source evidence from grep/read/git
diffs at the affected code site. A random SHA string in a random file is never
invalidating evidence by itself.
If KIND is prose, treat the target text as the problem description and gather code
context yourself via source/read/git followups.
semcode-backed source/type/callgraph lookups are helpers, not proof of absence.
They can be unavailable while indexing and can miss macros, globals, and complex
definitions. If semcode cannot find or parse a symbol, use read/search/grep against
the worktree before treating required source as missing or a symbol/path as absent.
For finding_dir inputs, affected file paths from metadata/FINDING/summary are direct
read targets; do not wait for semcode before reading those files.
Always set research_status, valid, invalid_evidence, invalid_evidence_kind,
and research_decision.
Use research_status=confirmed and valid=true only when gathered source proves a
concrete bug exists at workspace HEAD and analysis contains a specific fix contract.
Use research_status=invalid and valid=false only with source/commit proof that the
bug is wrong. Use research_status=unconfirmed and valid=false when the bug may be
real but gathered evidence does not prove it, when required source is unavailable
after direct read/search fallback has also failed,
or when the finding needs more audit work before patching. Do not route unconfirmed
research to write-patch.
Proving a concrete bug requires proving the alleged state is valid and reachable,
not merely that one local function would mishandle that state if it appeared. For
each required flag combination, object state, lock state, refcount state, callback
ordering, or lifetime transition, inspect the creators/converters and validators of
that state. If the current tree's assertions, WARN/VM_WARN paths, page-table checks,
type contracts, helper comments, or documented API rules reject the alleged state,
treat that as invalidating evidence when the contradiction is decisive; otherwise
mark research unconfirmed and request the missing evidence.
If the proposed fix restores behavior that current history deliberately removed,
read that removal commit and require concrete evidence that the removal was wrong
or incomplete before confirming. A patch must not be planned only to handle an
invalid or deliberately forbidden state.
A confirmed result needs a concrete trigger path: creator path -> transformed state
-> affected function -> violated contract/bad outcome. If any link is speculative,
set research_status=unconfirmed unless source/commit evidence proves the state is
impossible or already fixed, in which case set research_status=invalid.
is_latent flags a real-but-unreachable bug. Set is_latent=true ONLY when (a) the
code is wrong by its own contract or API rules and the fix is worth taking, AND
(b) no caller, configuration, or runtime path in the current tree reaches the
wrong-state condition. Typical cases: dead-but-incorrect helper, defensive cleanup
for a branch the current callers never take, or a contract violation that only a
future caller would expose. A latent bug still requires bug_proven=true; the
concrete trigger requirement above is relaxed to "contract violation" only when
is_latent=true. Cite the absence of triggers in analysis (e.g. "only caller X
always passes Y, so the bad branch is unreachable today"). Leave is_latent=false
when any reachable trigger exists, even an unusual or hard-to-hit one. Latent bugs
get a prominent "latent bug" notice as the first body paragraph of the commit
message by write-commit-message; do not set is_latent=true to soften a normal fix.
Use invalid_evidence="" and invalid_evidence_kind=none when research_status is
confirmed or unconfirmed, or whenever you do not have source/commit proof that the
bug is invalid.
research_decision is the structured rationale for routing. Keep it consistent with
research_status:
- confirmed: bug_proven=true, fix_contract_proven=true, invalidity_proven=false, needs_more_audit=false.
- invalid: bug_proven=false, fix_contract_proven=false, invalidity_proven=true, needs_more_audit=false.
- unconfirmed: invalidity_proven=false, and at least one of bug_proven/fix_contract_proven is false or needs_more_audit=true.
Followups have a single workflow meaning: a blocking followup (`nice_to_have` omitted
or false) is a request for another gather round. Emitting one fails this step's eval
regardless of status, and the runner re-runs research with the gathered evidence; that
is how you ask for more rounds. A nice-to-have followup (`nice_to_have: true`) is a
deferred audit suggestion that does not block the eval — use this for the "would be
nice to double-check later" notes you would otherwise hide in analysis prose, and
ship them alongside any terminal status. Reach a terminal status only when you have
no blocking followups left.
Do not use words like confirmed, verified, proved, or definitely in analysis for an
unconfirmed result; say evidence suggests or not proven instead. Rust routes only
from structured fields, but the prose should not contradict them.
Pull every file the bug touches, every caller of the affected symbols, and enough local
history to understand whether the bug is real and how to fix it. Do not do an exhaustive
Fixes: tag search in this step; a dedicated fixes-tag-search step owns provenance after
the patch exists.
If the bug is invalid (already fixed by a different commit, unreachable path, misread
semantics), set research_status=invalid, valid=false,
invalid_evidence_kind=source_or_commit_evidence, and put the evidence in
invalid_evidence. Cite a file:line or commit ref that existed
BEFORE this run started. Read/access/context failures are not invalid_evidence; do not
mark them invalid.

research_status.description: confirmed means a concrete bug and fix contract were proven; invalid means source/commit evidence disproves the bug; unconfirmed means do not patch yet.

valid.description: Compatibility mirror: true only when research_status=confirmed.

invalid_evidence.description: file:line or commit ref proving the bug is wrong; empty when valid=true.

invalid_evidence_kind.description: source_or_commit_evidence means invalid_evidence is actionable proof, not an access or context failure; none otherwise.

followups.description: Typed followups emitted by the slow agent. Each entry must satisfy the Followup schema (kind/name required). Set `nice_to_have: true` on entries that are deferred audits (would be nice to double-check, but the current verdict does not depend on them). Omit or set `nice_to_have: false` for blocking evidence requests; the eval rejects any terminal status while a blocking followup is present.

fix_plan.description: Ordered series plan. Each item is one independent commit todo with id, title, scope, affected_files, affected_symbols, fix_contract, rationale, and depends_on.

bug_inventory.description: Immutable original bug identities. Required for confirmed planning research; separate from commit-oriented fix_plan todos.

plan_update.description: Revision-checked atomic mutation of current or pending series work. Valid only for unconfirmed per-todo research.

research_decision.description: Structured routing rationale. Must agree with research_status and valid; do not rely on analysis prose for routing.

is_latent.description: True only when the bug is real (the code violates its own contract) but no reachable caller, config, or runtime path triggers it in the current tree. Causes write-commit-message to insert a 'latent bug with no known triggers' notice as the first body paragraph (after the subject and blank line).

steps.title: Record per-bug invalidation evidence in metadata.yaml
Check kernel mailing-list archive for an existing fix
prompt: Step LORE: SEARCH FOR EXISTING PATCHES.
Search the kernel mailing-list archive (lore) for a recent patch that already
fixes this bug. The lore tool runs a body regex search restricted to the last
30 days (the runner sets the date window automatically; you do not need to pass it).
BUG INPUT: {{workflow.target}}
KIND: {{workflow.target_kind}}
RESEARCH ANALYSIS:
{{research.analysis || ''}}
AFFECTED FILES:
{{research.affected_files}}
AFFECTED SYMBOLS:
{{research.affected_symbols}}
BUGS (from metadata.bugs / research.fix_plan):
{{research.fix_plan || ''}}
Pick 2-4 short body-search queries. Each query should target ONE of:
- an affected function or struct name from research.affected_symbols
- a distinctive helper or API call that the buggy code path uses
- a short phrase combining the subsystem and the observed symptom
Avoid one-word generic queries (`cpu`, `bpf`) and avoid full sentences. Each
query is passed as a regex body pattern; plain identifiers and short phrases
match themselves, but escape regex metacharacters (`.`, `(`, `[`, `+`, `?`)
if you want them literal. Issue each query as a `lore` followup. Inspect the
returned threads — read the patch hunks via `read`
or `git` followups if needed — and decide whether any thread proposes the same
fix this run is about to write.
Return an analysis paragraph describing what queries you ran, what threads you
inspected, and which (if any) propose the same fix. Populate existing_patches[]
with one entry per plausible match. duplicate_proven=true ONLY when a posted
patch addresses the same code site with the same semantic change and is plainly
intended to fix this bug (not a related one); cite a msgid + subject so a human
can verify. Do not block the workflow on uncertain matches — set
duplicate_proven=false and put the candidate(s) in existing_patches[] with a
relevance score so write-patch can still see them.
Do not treat a matching SHA or subject as sufficient on its own; an existing-patch
match requires the subject/message and the actual patch semantics to match the
affected code site.
If lore is unavailable (the MCP tool returns an error or the server isn't
wired), record that in the analysis and return empty existing_patches[] +
duplicate_proven=false. Do not invent threads.

existing_patches.description: Lore threads that may propose the same fix. msgid is the Message-ID; url is the lore.kernel.org permalink if available; relevance is a short prose note about why this thread matches.

duplicate_proven.description: True only when a posted upstream patch demonstrably proposes the same fix at the same site. Triggers a `duplicate` outcome entry in metadata.yaml.results, but does NOT block the workflow — write-patch still runs.

analysis.description: Free-text summary of queries run and what was inspected.

steps.title: Write the patch
prompt: Step 2: WRITE PATCH ONLY.
ORCHESTRATOR INSTRUCTION (if non-empty, follow it verbatim — the orchestrator routed back to write-patch with this guidance):
{{orchestrator.instruction || ''}}
GATHER REQUIREMENT FOR ORCHESTRATOR-NAMED SYMBOLS — read before deciding ready_for_slow:

When the ORCHESTRATOR INSTRUCTION above names specific functions, helpers, structs, fields, or file:line callsites, the fast-gather phase MUST have the verbatim source of those symbols in its accumulated context before setting `ready_for_slow=true`. The orchestrator can only PROSE-describe what a function does or what a struct contains; that description is unverifiable from the slow-agent's seat without the actual code. Without source in context, the slow agent guesses at lifetime, refcount, locking, ordering, or ABI semantics and emits kerneldoc/comment/changelog claims that look plausible but are factually wrong. Each such wrong claim costs a full review fan-out + orchestrator cycle to catch and re-route; repeated misses can exhaust the orchestrator's attempt budget on a single defect.
Concretely, for every distinct symbol the instruction names:
1. Check the complete accumulated `symbols` and `context` first — if the body is already present, you're done for that symbol.

2. Otherwise emit `source:<symbol>` (or `type:<name>` for a struct/union/typedef). If semcode returns nothing, fall back to `read:<file>:<line>+<lines>` using a file path the instruction gave you (or the affected_files list).
3. Do NOT set `ready_for_slow=true` until the current symbols/context cover every symbol the instruction named.
Trust the orchestrator's prose for routing intent (which defect to fix, what shape the fix should take); verify its factual claims about a symbol's body by fetching that body.
RESEARCH RESULT:
- affected files: {{research.affected_files}}
- affected symbols: {{research.affected_symbols}}
BROADER FIX SERIES PLAN:
{{research.fix_plan || workflow.fix_series_plan || ''}}
CURRENT FIX TODO:
{{workflow.current_fix_todo || ''}}
RESEARCH ANALYSIS / FIX SKETCH:
{{research.analysis || ''}}
EXISTING UPSTREAM PATCHES, IF ANY (from the lore-search step):
- duplicate proven: {{lore-search.duplicate_proven || 'false'}}
- matching threads: {{lore-search.existing_patches || '[]'}}
- analysis: {{lore-search.analysis || ''}}
Use this to AVOID inventing a different fix than the upstream community already
settled on. When duplicate_proven is true, you may still write the patch (the
operator wants the local artifact), but cite the upstream Message-ID in the
commit message so the trailer carries `Link: <lore url>`.
PRIOR WRITE-PATCH ATTEMPTS IN THIS RUN (oldest first; empty on first attempt):
{{write-patch.prior_attempts || ''}}
If non-empty, each entry is a previous slow-agent output for this same step that the
workflow rejected (eval failure, build failure, or review-driven branch back). Read
what was tried and why it was rejected; do not propose a structurally different patch
shape on every retry — that is fix-shape thrashing, not progress. Address the latest
concrete defect rather than abandoning the prior approach. If a fundamentally new shape
is genuinely needed, explicitly justify it in analysis with cited source or review
evidence that rules the prior shape out.
RECONCILED REVIEW INSTRUCTIONS (authoritative when non-empty):
The review lenses ran in parallel and could not see each other, so reconcile-review
merged their duplicates, resolved their contradictions, and dropped what the source
disproved or the fix contract put out of scope. Work the `target: source` entries in
the order given. Do NOT reopen a resolved contradiction or reinstate a dropped defect;
if you believe a resolution is wrong, say so in review_dispute with cited source.
Each entry carries a `kind`. `behavior` means executable code must change — a comment
or kerneldoc edit does not discharge it, and the reviewer will raise it again.
`documentation` means comment/kerneldoc text only: make that edit and do not alter
behavior under cover of it.
{{reconcile-review.instructions || '[]'}}
Behaviors the reconciliation judged correct as written, so only their description was
changed. If you find one of these judgements is wrong, do not silently fix the code:
say so in review_dispute with the source that contradicts it.
{{reconcile-review.behavior_accepted || '[]'}}
How reconcile-review resolved the lens conflicts, and what it dropped:
{{reconcile-review.contradictions || '[]'}}
{{reconcile-review.dropped || '[]'}}
PATCH FEEDBACK FROM PRIOR BUILD OR REVIEW ATTEMPT, IF ANY:
{{compile-triage.analysis || ''}}
The raw per-lens defects below are context for the reconciled instructions above,
not a second worklist. When they disagree, the reconciled set wins.
{{review.source_defects || ''}}
LOOP OBJECTIVES (what this fix must make true, carried across review cycles, with how
many cycles each has been open). The reconciliation pass owns these:
{{objectives.list || '[]'}}
MUST FIX -- when non-empty, this objective id is the only thing that matters this round;
everything else waits until it lands:
{{reconcile-review.must_fix || ''}}
SCOPE AMENDMENT to the fix contract, in force for the rest of this fix:
{{reconcile-review.scope_amendment || ''}}
If MUST FIX is set, make it land in this pass. Do not spend the pass on anything else.
Use this ledger as review history. Address open source/build/behavior entries for the
current fix todo, and if you dispute one, put the evidence in review_dispute instead
of re-editing unrelated code.
This step receives only source/build/behavior defects. Commit-message-only review
defects are routed to write-commit-message and are intentionally not included here.
If no concrete source/build/behavior defect is present, do not invent one.
If prior review source_defects are present but the current patch already satisfies them,
do not emit fake edits. Emit no code_edits/code_output, set review_dispute to a concise
evidence-based explanation of why the review defect is invalid, and cite the current
source/control-flow facts the review should re-check. Only use review_dispute to answer
a prior review defect; do not use it for build failures or fresh patch writing.
Before editing, fetch the verbatim current contents of every function you will change.
Use read followups for affected files; do not rely on source for affected files after
any edit/commit because symbol indexes can be stale. On retry after build or review
feedback, inspect git diff HEAD~1 and read the current worktree bytes before emitting
code_edits. Every old_string in code_edits must come from the file as it actually is on
disk and must match exactly once unless replace_all=true is intentional for every
matching occurrence. If old_string appears more than once, include more surrounding
unchanged context so the edit is unique.
Emit code_edits for the current fix todo only. Do not opportunistically fix sibling
todos from the broader series, even if the files overlap; those will run through
their own write/build/review/publish budgets. Each code_edits item must use this shape:
{"file_path": "path/to/file.c", "old_string": "...", "new_string": "..."}. Do not use
source-symbol field names such as `filename` in code_edits. Do not write
.kres-commit-msg.tmp here. Do not run git commit. In kernel workspaces, if you know
the primary object file, return it as build_target; otherwise the runner derives it from
the changed .c/.S paths. In non-kernel workspaces, leave build_target empty so the
workspace build step uses that project's normal build command.
For header-only, documentation-only, Kconfig-only, or other non-object kernel changes,
leave build_target empty; the deterministic build step will skip cleanly when no enabled
object target can be derived from the actual git diff.
In kernel workspaces, the reaper will add all other changed .c objects from the actual
git diff and skip targets disabled by the current Kconfig.

build_target.description: Kernel object file path for the make step, e.g. path/to/file.o. Leave empty outside kernel workspaces. Machine-filled from changed kernel source paths when omitted.

changed_files.description: Machine-populated non-message paths emitted by this write-patch attempt.

code_changes_emitted.description: Machine-populated true when this attempt emitted code_edits or non-message code_output for at least one path.

affected_files_changed.description: Machine-populated true when the non-message paths emitted by this attempt have an unstaged diff after code_edits/code_output are applied.

review_dispute.description: Empty for normal patch writes. Non-empty when the model rejected the prior review's source-defect on evidence (no edits needed). The orchestrator reads this when deciding whether to keep iterating or publish.

steps.title: Search for the introducing commit
prompt: Step 3: FIXES TAG SEARCH ONLY.
Your only job is to search for the commit that introduced the bug fixed by the current
patch. Do not edit files. Do not write a commit message. Do not review patch correctness
except as needed to understand the buggy invariant.
BUG INPUT:
{{workflow.target}}
BROADER FIX SERIES PLAN:
{{research.fix_plan || workflow.fix_series_plan || ''}}
CURRENT FIX TODO:
{{workflow.current_fix_todo || ''}}
RESEARCH ANALYSIS:
{{research.analysis || ''}}
AFFECTED FILES:
{{research.affected_files}}
AFFECTED SYMBOLS:
{{research.affected_symbols}}
PATCH UNDER CONSTRUCTION:
Use readonly git followups to inspect the full patch under construction, plus the
affected functions and their callers. On the first patch attempt, `git diff` shows the
uncommitted patch. On retry after build or review feedback, a prior attempt may already
be committed and the worktree diff may show only the incremental correction; in that
case inspect `git diff HEAD~1` as the full patch relative to the original base, and also
inspect `git diff` for the latest uncommitted correction. Do not base provenance on the
incremental retry diff alone.
FIXES TAG RESEARCH IS CAREFUL HISTORY RESEARCH. The goal is the commit that introduced
the bug, not the last commit that touched or moved the current line. `git blame` is only
a starting point. Kernel code is often renamed, folio-converted, split, moved, or
mechanically rewritten; do not use blame alone as fixes_sha.
Try hard before giving up:
- Inspect the full patch to identify the exact buggy invariant fixed by this patch.
- Run blame for the affected lines, but treat blame results as candidates only.
- Inspect candidate diffs with `git show`.
- Follow moved or renamed code with `git log --follow -- <path>` where useful.

- Bound every history request. A patch-bearing log over a whole file (`git log -p -- <path>`, with or without --follow) returns every patch ever applied to it; on a long-lived file that is megabytes and can exceed the model's entire input budget by itself, failing the step. Ask for what identifies a commit -- `--oneline` to list, `-S`/`-G` to find it, `-n` to bound the count -- and read one patch body with `git show <sha>` once you know which commit you want.
- Use pickaxe searches (`git log -S` / `git log -G`) for the affected function names, helper calls, field names, missing cleanup call, and distinctive surrounding code.
- For each plausible candidate, prove the invariant changed across that commit: the preimage must lack the bug or lack the affected path, and the postimage must contain the buggy state.
- If multiple functions have different introducing commits, choose the earliest commit that introduced a real instance fixed by this patch and explain why.
Set fixes_sha and fixes_subject only when the evidence is concrete enough for a kernel
Fixes: trailer. If no candidate is proven with certainty, leave fixes_sha empty and fill
unproven_fixes_candidates with the best plausible commits you checked. A wrong Fixes:
tag is worse than no Fixes: trailer.
Return concise analysis describing what history searches you ran, what candidate diffs
you inspected, and why the proven commit is correct or why each candidate remains
unproven.

fixes_sha.description: 12+ char SHA of the proven introducing commit, empty when unproven.

fixes_subject.description: Exact subject line of the proven introducing commit.

fixes_evidence.description: Concise proof that the chosen commit introduced the buggy invariant.

unproven_fixes_candidates.description: Plausible but unproven commits, formatted as '<sha> ("<subject>") - <why unproven>'.

analysis.description: History search narrative and candidate evaluation.

steps.title: Write the commit message
prompt: Step 4: WRITE COMMIT MESSAGE ONLY.
ORCHESTRATOR INSTRUCTION (if non-empty, follow it verbatim — the orchestrator routed back to write-commit-message with this guidance):
{{orchestrator.instruction || ''}}
Use readonly git diff/show/log followups if you need to inspect the patch. Write
.kres-commit-msg.tmp via code_output in this turn. Do not edit kernel source in this
step. Do not emit git add, git commit, git commit --amend, make, or publish followups;
deterministic reaper steps own those actions.
RESEARCH ANALYSIS:
{{research.analysis || ''}}
BROADER FIX SERIES PLAN:
{{research.fix_plan || workflow.fix_series_plan || ''}}
CURRENT FIX TODO:
{{workflow.current_fix_todo || ''}}
FIXES TAG SEARCH RESULT:
- proven fixes sha: {{fixes-tag-search.fixes_sha || ''}}
- proven fixes subject: {{fixes-tag-search.fixes_subject || ''}}
- proof: {{fixes-tag-search.fixes_evidence || ''}}
- potential but unproven candidates: {{fixes-tag-search.unproven_fixes_candidates || ''}}
- search analysis: {{fixes-tag-search.analysis || ''}}
RECONCILED REVIEW INSTRUCTIONS (authoritative when non-empty):
The review lenses ran in parallel and could not see each other, so reconcile-review
merged their duplicates, resolved their contradictions, and dropped what the source
disproved or the fix contract put out of scope. Work the `target: commit_message`
entries in the order given, and do not reinstate a dropped defect.
{{reconcile-review.instructions || '[]'}}
How reconcile-review resolved the lens conflicts, and what it dropped:
{{reconcile-review.contradictions || '[]'}}
{{reconcile-review.dropped || '[]'}}
COMMIT-MESSAGE FEEDBACK FROM PRIOR REVIEW ATTEMPT, IF ANY:
The raw per-lens defects below are context for the reconciled instructions above,
not a second worklist. When they disagree, the reconciled set wins.
{{review.commit_message_defects || ''}}
LOOP OBJECTIVES (what this fix must make true, carried across review cycles, with how
many cycles each has been open). The reconciliation pass owns these:
{{objectives.list || '[]'}}
MUST FIX -- when non-empty, this objective id is the only thing that matters this round;
everything else waits until it lands:
{{reconcile-review.must_fix || ''}}
SCOPE AMENDMENT to the fix contract, in force for the rest of this fix:
{{reconcile-review.scope_amendment || ''}}
If MUST FIX is set and it is not a changelog objective, say so in analysis rather
than rewriting the message around it.
Use this ledger as review history. Address open commit-message/trailer entries for the
current fix todo, but do not make source changes here.
ASSISTED-BY TRAILER:
- The commit message MUST include exactly this trailer line:
`Assisted-by: {{workflow.assisted_by}}`
- Do not emit any other Assisted-by value.
LATENT BUG NOTICE:
- research.is_latent for this run: {{research.is_latent || 'false'}}
- When research.is_latent is true, the commit body's FIRST paragraph
(immediately after the subject line and the blank line that follows it) MUST
consist of exactly this verbatim line, on its own, with no prefix, suffix, or
rewording:
`Note: This fixes a latent bug with no known triggers in the kernel today.`
A blank line follows that paragraph, then the regular body continues. The
subject line itself is the normal kernel subject — do not put the notice on
line 1, because git treats line 1 as the subject and `git log --oneline`,
`git format-patch`, and lore archives would then show the notice instead of
the actual fix.
- When research.is_latent is false or absent, omit the latent notice entirely.
Do not add it to non-latent fixes.
COMMIT MESSAGE RULES:
- Subject and body follow COMMIT MESSAGE STYLE.

- The raw git commit subject (line 1) MUST be <=55 chars including the subsystem prefix, so the full generated `Subject: [PATCH] <subject>` line is <=72 chars including the literal word `Subject`. This cap applies to every commit, latent or not; the latent notice does not move or replace the subject.
- HARD WRAP prose at 75 columns. Trailers and indented code are exempt.
- Write a human-readable kernel changelog, not a dense proof memo or review transcript.

- Use the non-prose descriptor catalog in COMMIT MESSAGE STYLE as the default way to state the failing path, consequence, and mechanism. Select the smallest applicable descriptor and use more than one only when each carries different information.

- Prose is supporting material only. Keep it as short as possible and use it only to set up a descriptor or describe why it matters. Do not restate a descriptor in prose. The required one-sentence fix paragraph is the only exception.

- Code excerpts that explain the bug MUST be verbatim source, preceded by filename:function, with enough enclosing control flow to locate the failing branch. Do not rename identifiers, change capitalization, simplify helpers, or attach invented comments to retained source lines. A standalone `[ ... ] // omitted: <reason>` marker may replace at least two consecutive lines of unrelated code; never omit one line, use source-language comment syntax for an omission, or omit relevant control flow or state changes. Every retained source line must remain exact. Pseudocode is allowed only for the solution and MUST be labeled `pseudocode`.
- Do not inventory every caller, export, fallback, or negative case unless it is needed to understand the bug or justify the fix.
- MUST NOT contain: attacker, exploit, malicious, vulnerability, privilege escalation, arbitrary code execution, security, payload.
- Every factual claim must be provable from the patch or gathered source. Be precise about mitigations and fallback cleanup paths; do not claim a leak or crash unless the code proves it.

- In a fix series, the commit message is for the current fix todo's patch only: before commit, the worktree/index diff against HEAD; after commit or during review rewrite, `git diff HEAD~1`. That parent already includes earlier todos in the series. Describe the bug and fix relative to that parent, not relative to the original pre-series tree.

- If the message mentions a sibling todo or earlier series commit, label it explicitly as earlier/later series context. Do not say a sibling change is absent from, newly added by, or still needed in the current tree unless that is true for the current patch's parent-to-child diff.

- Do not paste stale pre-series source snippets or ASCII traces for code already changed by an earlier series commit. If historical pre-series behavior is needed to explain why this commit exists, say it was the pre-series state and keep the current commit's actual diff as the focus.
- Assisted-by trailer is REQUIRED.
- Add a Fixes: trailer only when proven fixes sha is non-empty. Format: `Fixes: <sha> ("<subject>")`.

- If proven fixes sha is empty, do not add a Fixes: trailer and do not mention unproven Fixes candidates in the changelog. Unproven history belongs in workflow analysis, not in the kernel commit message.
- On retry after review, fix the specific commit-message defects. Do not introduce new mechanism claims, extra caller inventories, or proof-memo prose to compensate for a review objection.

commit_message_written.description: Machine-populated true when this attempt wrote .kres-commit-msg.tmp via code_output.

code_changes_emitted.description: Machine-populated true when this attempt also emitted source code_edits (write-commit-message runs in coding mode and can fold doc-only or comment-only source edits into a commit-message rewrite). Used by review lens skip_if to decide whether source-correctness lenses must re-run: when the orchestrator routes here AND this is false, source did not change this cycle and the source lenses can skip.

analysis.description: Slow agent's narrative for this attempt. Surfaced to the orchestrator on a failed attempt so it can see WHY no commit message was written — empty bool + empty analysis really is silence, but a populated analysis often names the missing piece.

followups.description: Typed followups the slow agent emitted when it could not write the message. Surfaced to the orchestrator so a worker that refused can name concrete missing context (the patch diff, a related commit, etc.) for the next instruction.

The deterministic workspace build step failed for `{{build.build_target}}`.
STDOUT:
{{build.stdout}}
STDERR:
{{build.stderr}}
